title: ParaJSCC: A Parameterized Framework for Reusable Multimodal Joint Source–Channel Coding
authors: Kemi Chen; Mingkai Chen; Youjia Chen; Qian Liu; Wei Gao; Tiesong Zhao
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
abstract: Multimodal signals, such as visual, audio, and tactile data, are increasingly maintained as persistent digital assets in immersive communication systems and digital twins. In these settings, the same multimodal content is repeatedly accessed by heterogeneous receivers with varying modality and bandwidth requirements. Existing compression and Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) methods typically follow a per-request encoding paradigm, resulting in redundant computation and low efficiency during repeated access. To address this issue, we propose ParaJSCC, a multimodal JSCC framework designed for reusable representation serving. ParaJSCC converts each multimodal sample offline at the cloud/content server into a compact, quantized parameter package, which is then stored at the edge serving node for low-latency access. During serving, only the subset required by the current request is transmitted over the wireless channel, followed by lightweight decoding at the receiver. The framework employs a progressive shared-private parameterization to support modality-selective transmission and scalable reconstruction under varying bandwidth constraints. Experiments on multimodal datasets show that ParaJSCC significantly reduces online latency (e.g., from 17.18 ms to 4.34 ms for image-only requests and from 43.96 ms to 11.21 ms for full multimodal requests) and transmission rate (by 47.8%--51.2% for selective requests), while maintaining strong reconstruction quality under noisy channels.

title: Semantic-Aware Communications in Industrial IoT:What Can Be Tested Today, and What Is Missing?
authors: Rute C. Sofia
abstract: Classical networks treat every bit as equally important, which wastes time and energy in factories and requires extra traffic engineering for critical traffic. Semantic communications send only what a task needs, but how can they be tested under realistic conditions? This paper examines what can be tested today in 6G industrial IoT, that is, networks of factory machines, robots, and sensors, and what is still missing. It introduces semantic importance, a score attached to each message that states how much the message matters, and uses it in a context-driven design to derive eight testing needs. Existing simulators, emulators, testbeds, codecs, and learning frameworks are assessed against these needs, which reveals five gaps. We propose a toolchain of four components built around the ns-3 simulator for simulated and emulated scenarios.

title: An intent aware framework for semantic edge intelligence in autonomous 6g UAV and vehicular networks
authors: Salma Begum; Mudassir Khan; G. Suresh Babu; S Raghavi; Sapiah Binti Sakri
abstract: In autonomous communication between unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and vehicles in emerging sixth-generation (6G) networks, intelligent edge computing is essential for reliable decision-making under rapidly changing network conditions. This paper presents SEM-EDGE-X, a semantic edge intelligence framework integrating semantic feature extraction, Bayesian priority prediction, adaptive edge-to-cloud routing, semantic memory-assisted decision-making, dynamic resource management, adaptive cold-start semantic fusion, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) validation, dynamic trust refinement, and Digital Twin simulation. Performance is evaluated using Python and SUMO mobility modelling with the KITTI and UAVDT datasets under varying channel conditions and network densities, in terms of semantic accuracy, simulated communication latency, throughput, energy consumption, scalability, computational cost, and robustness. The results indicate a favourable trade-off among communication efficiency, energy consumption, and semantic performance, with 95.76% semantic accuracy (transmission fidelity under channel noise, not correctness against ground-truth labels), approximately 1.04 ms simulated communication latency (propagation, transmission, and queueing only), throughput above 25 Mbps, and energy consumption below 0.006 mJ. The separately measured software execution time of the pipeline is approximately 109.6 ms and is not included in the simulated latency.

title: QISFP: a quantum-inspired semantic fidelity protocol for energy-efficient and noise-resilient visual IoT transmission
authors: David Elias Emmanuel; Anil Fernando
abstract: Visual Internet of Things deployments operate under coupled bandwidth, energy and channel-reliability constraints, yet conventional video coding optimises pixel-level reconstruction rather than the preservation of task-relevant meaning. This paper presents QISFP, a quantum-inspired semantic fidelity protocol that treats semantic degradation as a stochastic state transformation rather than as additive signal distortion. It couples delta encoding of temporally associated object-level semantic states with a stochastic channel built from classical analogues of the depolarizing and amplitude-damping maps, and reconstructs meaning by energy- and confidence-weighted fusion over a temporal window. The framework is classical throughout: the quantum formalism supplies trace-preserving maps whose diagonal restriction is a stochastic matrix, which keeps per-object cost linear rather than quadratic in the semantic dimension. The induced class channel is shown to be $$M$$ M -ary symmetric, yielding two independent decay constants that characterise a semantic link and fix a multi-hop relaying budget, while a source-channel separation argument gives the attainability limit $$F \le 1 - p_d(1-1/M)$$ F ≤ 1 - p d ( 1 - 1 / M ) , met with equality by uncoded single-observation transmission; every attainable gain therefore lies in the temporal dimension. Simulation on CDNet 2014 and UCF-101 indicates 27.5% lower energy per frame and 30.3% lower transmitted volume than full-frame x264, with semantic fidelity of 0.922 against 0.855 for a frame-wise semantic baseline, at a cost of 1.28 dB in PSNR. An end-to-end measurement on detector output tests the theory directly: the frame-wise baseline tracks the single-use limit to within 0.022 IoU, the framework exceeds that limit wherever the channel is non-trivial, and at matched fidelity it requires between 42% and 64% fewer bits than the baseline. The protocol requires a few kilobytes of state and fewer than $$10^4$$ 10 4 operations per frame, so embedded feasibility is governed by the choice of semantic extractor rather than by QISFP itself.

title: Adaptive Channel Coding with Semantic-Aware Error Protection for 6G Non-Terrestrial Networks
authors: Ambar Bajpai
abstract: Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) — comprising low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) — are increasingly regarded as a foundational layer of sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, extending connectivity to rural, maritime, and disaster-affected regions that remain beyond the economic reach of terrestrial infrastructure. NTN links, however, present a uniquely hostile channel environment: long and time-varying propagation delay, large Doppler shifts induced by high relative platform velocity, deep fades from atmospheric and rain attenuation, and severe constraints on onboard power and computation. Conventional fixed-rate or classically-adaptive channel coding schemes, which react only to instantaneous signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), are poorly matched to this environment: they either over-provision redundancy, wasting scarce bandwidth and energy, or under-provision it and trigger the so-called cliff effect, in which a small SNR drop causes catastrophic decoding failure. In this paper we propose semantic-aware adaptive channel coding (SA-ACC), a framework that couples semantic importance estimation with rate- and redundancy-adaptive coding so that error-protection resources are allocated according to the task-relevant meaning of transmitted content rather than uniformly across all bits. We formalize the system model for a representative NTN scenario — a LEO downlink relayed through a HAPS node — define a semantic importance metric derived from task-gradient sensitivity, and design a two-stage adaptation control loop that jointly selects code rate, modulation order, and per-feature protection level under explicit delay and energy budgets. We further specify a complete evaluation methodology, comparing SA-ACC against fixed-rate LDPC/polar coding, conventional adaptive coding and modulation (ACM), and non-semantic deep joint source-channel coding (JSCC) across bit error rate, block error rate, semantic fidelity, throughput, latency, and energy metrics, and use this methodology to reason about SA-ACC’s expected behavior ahead of full numerical validation. Our architectural analysis indicates that SA-ACC should be able to sustain task-relevant reconstruction quality at lower effective SNR than baselines optimized purely at the bit level, at the cost of additional encoder and decoder complexity that we discuss explicitly. We close by outlining the simulation and ablation study required to convert this design-and-methodology contribution into a fully validated result.

title: Leakage-Aware Encrypted Semantic Communication with Key-Conditioned Signal Perturbation
authors: Omar Kaaki; Maria Slim; Mariette Awad; Hadi Sarieddeen
abstract: Encrypted semantic communication systems protect transmitted messages by inserting key-conditioned modules into a deep-learning semantic communication pipeline, but existing designs rely on a fixed adversarial weight and operate mainly at the semantic-feature level. We propose two changes to the encrypted semantic communication system (ESCS): a key-conditioned signal-domain perturbation layer, called learned adversarial perturbation injection (LAPI), and an information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE)-guided adaptive training rule that {adds an adaptive leakage penalty alongside the fixed adversarial objective} using an InfoNCE-based proxy for mutual information leakage. Experiments on the Europarl corpus over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading channels show that InfoNCE-guided training is the primary source of eavesdropper suppression, reducing the eavesdropper's bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) score to approximately 0.07 at high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Adding LAPI to the InfoNCE-guided objective further lowers the InfoNCE-estimated leakage by 5-9% with low measured inference overhead, while its impact on legitimate-receiver BLEU depends on channel conditions. The two mechanisms operate on different parts of the pipeline and can be jointly applied.

title: Resource Allocation for Semantic‐Driven Multibeam Satellite Systems via Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jianpeng Xu; Shuang Li; Xuehu Wang
abstract: This paper focuses on resource allocation in a semantic‐driven multibeam geostationary earth orbit (GEO) satellite system. The sum semantic rate (SSR) is maximized by jointly designing the subchannel and power allocation, while satisfying the semantic similarity. Since the optimization problem is non‐convex and mathematically intractable, an algorithm based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL), specifically the softmax deep double deterministic policy gradients with prioritized experience replay (SD3‐PER) algorithm, is proposed to maximize the reward through sustained interaction with the semantic‐driven multibeam GEO satellite environment. Simulation findings demonstrate that the proposed scheme can achieve higher SSR than the benchmark algorithms.

title: AI-ENABLED SEMANTIC COMMUNICATION ARCHITECTURE FOR 6G NETWORKS: AN INTELLIGENT, CONTEXT-AWARE AND RESOURCE-EFFICIENT FRAMEWORK WITH HYBRID OPTIMIZATION
authors: Ganesan S.; Jagatheeshkumar G.
venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive
abstract: Communication architectures that can enable intelligent services, vast connectivity, ultra-low latency, and extremely heterogeneous applications are necessary due to the sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks' rapid expansion. Large amounts of redundant data are communicated with significant bandwidth, energy, and computational overhead since conventional communication systems are primarily concerned with correct bit-level transmission. By conveying task-relevant meaning rather than full raw data, semantic communication overcomes this constraint. This research presents an AI-Enabled Semantic Communication Architecture for 6G Networks that combines context-aware decision-making, intelligent semantic extraction, and hybrid optimization. Gray Wolf Optimization (GWO) optimizes transmission parameters and semantic reconstruction quality, whereas Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) selects semantic features and allocates communication resources in the suggested framework. The optimization method is dynamically modified by a context-aware semantic controller based on network resources, channel conditions, and application needs. The framework is intended to maximize semantic similarity and communication efficiency while minimizing semantic distortion, latency, energy usage, and bandwidth utilization. Text-based semantic communication is used in an experimental assessment framework with different network loads and signal-to-noise ratios. For upcoming 6G applications, the suggested architecture offers a basis for resource-efficient, flexible, and intelligent semantic communication.

title: SIRAZ: Sparse Inter-Layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-Shot Visual Neural Decoding
authors: Neha; Mudasir Ganaie
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces aim to establish direct communication between neural activity and external systems, making interpretation of brain signals an important problem. In this context, neural visual decoding seeks to infer visual information from neural activity by learning a mapping between brain responses and the corresponding visual stimuli. It investigates how visual information emerges from neural signals and relates to perceptual processing while enabling the reconstruction or retrieval of visual stimuli from neural signals. Our brain primarily follows a hierarchical pathway to process visual information captured by the eye. However, neural representations learned by existing methods differ fundamentally from those produced by the biological visual system. To bridge this gap and mimic the human vision hierarchy, we introduce Sparse Inter-layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-shot (SIRAZ). SIRAZ is a framework that aligns neural visual representations by jointly modeling early visual processes via fovea- and magnocellular-pathway-inspired Difference-of-Gaussians transformations. To align the semantic information with neural information, it extracts multiple intermediate representations of the image at multiple depths and passes them through the Residual Gated Adapter Mechanism. To study the temporal dynamics of neural signals, the Direction-aware Multi-Scale Temporal Attention Encoder is introduced to align the learned neural representation with the final visual representation. The proposed framework achieves 92.5% top-1 and 99.27% top-5 accuracy in the intra-subject setting on the THINGS-EEG dataset, and 50.25% and 75% top-1 and top-5 accuracy in the THINGS-MEG dataset. The results indicate that combining biologically motivated visual representations with the structured modalities of neural dynamics improves cross-modal alignment and zero-shot image retrieval.

title: Physical Layer Security for Digital Semantic Communication: A Bit-Level Perspective
authors: Seonjung Kim; Jaehyeok Kim; Yo-Seb Jeon
abstract: Digital semantic communication requires reliable recovery of task-relevant information at a legitimate receiver while limiting source reconstruction by an eavesdropper. Uniform bit protection, however, does not account for the heterogeneous reliability and secrecy requirements of semantic bits. This paper proposes a bit-level physical layer security (PLS) framework that learns these requirements and incorporates them into physical-layer resource allocation. We first introduce a wiretap semantic feature channel whose two-stage training learns per-bit target bit-flip probabilities for the legitimate receiver (Bob) and the eavesdropper (Eve). These targets characterize the reliability requirements at Bob and the secrecy protection requirements against Eve. Based on the learned targets, we formulate a joint power and artificial-noise (AN) allocation problem for a multiple-input single-output wiretap channel under a worst-case angular-separation model. For a given target profile, the optimal information-AN power split admits a closed-form solution, and the per-bit power allocation is obtained by water-filling. We further develop a leakage-aware selection method among multiple learned-target profiles and extend the design to multiple-input multiple-output channels. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a better trade-off between preserving reconstruction quality at Bob and degrading that at Eve than uniform power allocation and the evaluated learning-based secure semantic communication schemes.

title: Drift-Aware Adaptive Semantic Codec Update Strategy for Dynamic Semantic Communications
authors: Bizhu Wang; Manqi Li; Shujun Han; Mengying Sun; Xiaodong Xu
abstract: Semantic communication reduces transmission overhead by conveying task-relevant semantic features, but its performance depends on the consistency between training and target-domain data distributions. In dynamic environments, distribution drift can make offline-trained semantic codec models stale and degrade transmission performance. Frequent updates alleviate this degradation but increase communication, computation, and queueing costs, whereas infrequent updates delay model adaptation. To address this tradeoff, we propose a drift-aware adaptive update strategy for dynamic semantic communication systems. Drift intensity is quantified in the semantic feature space, and Drift-Aware Age of Model (DA-AoM) is introduced to jointly capture drift-induced performance degradation, drift-dependent update service delay, and conventional update latency. Closed-form average DA-AoM expressions are derived for edge-layer M/M/1 and cloud-layer D/M/1 update scenarios, based on which the update frequency is optimized under the queueing-stability constraint. Simulations show that DA-AoM captures the joint effects of drift intensity, computing rate, bandwidth, and update frequency on model freshness beyond conventional Age of Information (AoI). The proposed strategy reduces average DA-AoM by 9.2\%--42.4\% compared with representative baselines under the same resource constraints.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
authors: Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas
abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

title: Wildfire-SSR: Geolocation-Aware Multimodal Fusion for Structure-Level Wildfire Risk Assessment
authors: Yu-Hsuan Ho; Yiming Xiao; Hao-En Lai; Ali Mostafavi; Samuel D. Brody
abstract: Structure-level wildfire vulnerability assessment is critical for reducing losses in wildland-urban interface communities, yet existing methods often fail to combine parcel-scale ignition pathways with community-scale geographic coverage. This study introduces Wildfire-SSR (Satellite and Street-view for wildfire Risk), a geolocation-aware multimodal framework that integrates macro-scale satellite context with micro-scale street-view evidence. A Vision-Language Model extracts wildfire-relevant building and site attributes from pre-event street-view panoramas and converts them into structured semantic text. These features are spatially aligned with satellite imagery through a decoupled cross-attention fusion decoder, while a frozen satellite-pretrained DINOv3 encoder captures overhead visual context. Alternative geolocation embedding strategies are evaluated to anchor text-derived features within each satellite patch. The framework is tested on approximately 37,000 structures affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles, using wildfire risk labels derived from relative post-event damage patterns to better represent inherent structural vulnerability. Rotary Positional Embedding provides the strongest spatial grounding, achieving a building localization F1 score of 0.6735 and a harmonic mean F1 score of 0.2476 for five-class pixel-level risk classification, outperforming unimodal baselines and an unanchored multimodal configuration. The model also shows a conservative bias in higher-risk classes, reducing severe-risk underestimation, and completes end-to-end assessment of the study area in 37 minutes on a single GPU. Wildfire-SSR reframes cross-view fusion as localized semantic alignment and provides a scalable tool for mitigation prioritization, resilience planning, and insurance-oriented wildfire risk assessment.

title: VISTA: A Framework for Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness
authors: Murat Arda Onsu; Poonam Lohan; Burak Kantarci; Aisha Syed; Matthew Andrews; Sean Kennedy
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks
authors: Kaiwen Yu; Gang Wu; Jiancun Fan; Saviour Zammit
abstract: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.

title: CableMoE: Harm-Regularized Mean-Residual Expert Fusion for Transmission-Corridor Segmentation
authors: Shima Salehi
abstract: Semantic mapping of transmission corridors benefits from heterogeneous LiDAR and image-guided predictors, but replacing a strong ensemble with a learned router can damage rare electrical assets. We introduce CableMoE, a post-hoc mixture of four frozen segmentation experts. Its deployable prediction is a calibrated residual around availability-aware probability averaging, while a harm penalty discourages extra loss on points that the mean already classifies correctly. A matched component study shows why each design choice is needed: an unconstrained learned mixture loses 1.032 mIoU points relative to probability mean, harm regularization restores 0.359 points at fixed capacity, and removing an unnecessary point-wise gate slightly improves accuracy and stability. With three zones for fitting, two disjoint zones for residual-strength selection, and router-untouched t5b5 for final reporting, CableMoE obtains 84.906% mIoU and 98.140 % overall accuracy. This is +10.000 points over SPT and +0.263 over probability mean; all three seeds improve the latter. Across pylon, conductor, structural-cable, and insulator classes, macro-IoU rises from 84.517% for SPT and 97.153% for probability mean to 98.144 %. The results support conservative residual composition, not a claim of a new segmentation backbone or universal state of the art

title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
authors: Zijia Cao; Hanqing Dou
abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.

title: DecompJSCC: Joint Source-Channel Coding With Decoupled SNR and Rate Adaptation
authors: Yunhao Liu; Jiancun Fan; Haojun Sun; Jie Luo
abstract: Deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) for image transmission must adapt to changes in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and available transmission resources. However, some existing joint-adaptive methods condition the encoder on the requested rate, while others apply static masks after encoding. The former couples latent formation to the rate request, whereas the latter cannot adapt channel selection to image content. To address these limitations, we propose DecompJSCC, which decomposes joint adaptation into SNR-conditioned latent formation and post-encoding rate control within a single model. The encoder applies SNR-conditioned block attention residuals across all stages, aggregating intra-stage and cross-stage semantic representations. At the receiver, an adapter performs SNR-conditioned affine correction. We introduce a post-encoding rate-adaptive channel semantic budgeting (RCSB) module whose shared gate selects channels of the formed latent by image content, adjusts their gains, and keeps exactly the requested count. This keeps the encoder output independent of the rate request for a fixed image and SNR. Experimental results show that DecompJSCC outperforms SwinJSCC and SA-RA-JSCC in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) across a range of SNR and rate settings, by 0.64 dB and 1.00 dB over SwinJSCC and by 0.97 dB and 0.96 dB over SA-RA-JSCC on Kodak and CLIC2021, while using only 7.5% of SwinJSCC's Adaptive ModNet parameters.

title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard
authors: Ragini Menon; Sabine Tittel
abstract: Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked. We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

title: Over-the-Air Computation for Imperfectly Synchronized Multi-View Semantic Communication
authors: Maximilian H. V. Tillmann; Julian Sündermann; Ahmad Halimi Razlighi; Edgar Beck; Armin Dekorsy
abstract: Compared to classical task-agnostic communication systems, which focus on reliable transmission of a message, semantic communication (SemCom) focuses on transmitting the task-relevant meaning behind the message. In this paper, we design a SemCom system for a distributed multi-view scenario, where multiple semantic devices observe a scene and collaborate through a single semantic receiver to execute a task. We propose adopting an Over-the-Air Computation (AirComp) channel for efficient use of resources, as AirComp uses a superposition of signals to directly compute a function, which in SemCom is decoding the semantic variable. However, AirComp relies heavily on perfect time and phase synchronization, which is not practical in real-world communication. We show that timing offsets of standards like 5G cause negligible degradation, and that larger timing offsets can be compensated by training. Nevertheless, the system cannot deal with the encountered levels of phase synchronization errors, even when trained with those levels of synchronization errors. Therefore, we propose integrating existing phase synchronization algorithms into the AirComp SemCom system training. Simulation results show that the proposed system can approach the task execution performance of a perfectly synchronized SemCom system.

title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
authors: Albert Shaju; Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas; Mingzhe Chen
abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.

title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
authors: Zhuoying Yang; Yichen Guo; Kathy Jia; Zichang Su; Ayesha Kashif; Nange Hai; Jeffrey Ming Han Li; Zhewen He; Silvio Kempf; Ni Jiachen; Junjie Yang; Muhammad Hamza; Zakaria El Ouahidi; Gabriel Azpitarte; Manling Li; Yi Fang; Shuhong Liu; Mengyu Wang
abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. Pretrained vision encoders already capture this information in their latent features, with CLIP linking objects to image regions, DINOv3 matching semantics across views, and VGGT encoding multi-view geometry. However, VLMs do not benefit from these features when we present them directly in context as grayscale feature images. We therefore propose LatentParse, a training-free framework that parses latent features into explicit spatial evidence for VLMs. In LatentParse, an analyst VLM probes the features of all three encoders with predefined tools that locate objects, track them across views, and measure motion between views. It then distills the results into a concise text report, which is provided together with the images to the VLM to answer the question. We evaluate LatentParse on MMSI-Bench, MV-RoboBench and SPAR-Bench, where it improves all five VLMs over the photo-only baseline by 0.7-2.4 percentage points on average. On MMSI-Bench, it raises Qwen3.8-27B from 34.4% to 39.5%, with the largest improvements of 19.2 percentage points on the camera-related questions. These results suggest that latent features become useful for spatial reasoning once they are parsed into relation evidence, without training. Code is available at https://github.com/Harvard-AI-and-Robotics-Lab/LatentParse.

title: CART: Clustering-based Analysis of Recurring narratives for Taxonomy construction
authors: Aggelos Semoglou; Thomas Tselentis; John Pavlopoulos
abstract: We present CART, a computational pipeline for extracting political narratives from parliamentary discourse and organizing them into a data-driven taxonomy without relying on predefined narrative categories. It encodes parliamentary discourse using semantic representations, filters relevant and reliable content through unsupervised confidence estimation, extracts narrative statements using LLMs, and uses narrative clustering and cluster analysis to construct a narrative taxonomy. Applied to Greek Parliament proceedings surrounding the 2023 Tempi train crash, it identifies ten recurring narrative families concerning responsibility attribution, institutional failure, railway safety, accountability, privatization, and the political interpretation of the tragedy. Our results demonstrate how combining unsupervised learning with LLM narrative extraction enables large parliamentary corpora to be transformed into interpretable, data-driven taxonomies of political narratives.

title: SIAMBA: A Pseudo-Siamese Mamba-based Deep Learning Network for Multimodal Flood Change Detection
authors: Muhammad Fasih Ishfaq; Giulio Weikmann; Lorenzo Bruzzone
abstract: Flood change detection from bi-temporal multispectral and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images is essential for rapid disaster response. In this context, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery provides discriminative spectral observations, whereas Sentinel-1 SAR provides weather-independent structural information. Using these modalities jointly requires modelling temporal evidence while accounting for cross-modal heterogeneity. In particular, change detection is complicated by cloud contamination, illumination variability, acquisition geometry and speckle, and heterogeneous land-cover responses. To address these challenges, we propose SIAMBA, a pseudo-siamese Mamba-based network for bi-temporal flood change detection from paired Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations. SIAMBA uses dedicated modality-specific encoders with dual-pooling squeeze-and-excitation recalibration and selective state-space processing for long-range spatial context. A gated cross-modal change module derives absolute, signed, and relative log-ratio differences at multiple semantic levels, and attention-refined skip connections support progressive multi-scale decoding. Experiments are carried out on OMBRIA benchmark, which includes an independent test set and geographically diverse subsets in France, Albania, Guyana, and Timor. SIAMBA achieves 81.98% IoU, and 93.57% OA on the independent test set, reaching the highest values in the considered comparison. It also provides the highest unweighted average IoU and OA across four regional subsets spatially disjuncted. These results indicate that combining selective state-space contextual modelling with gated multiscale discrepancy learning effectively improves flood change mapping across the evaluated geographic settings.

title: Learning Dense Head-Object Contact Estimation with Synthetic Data
authors: Daniel Sungho Jung; Kyoung Mu Lee
abstract: Head serves a critical role in human cognitive and perceptual functions while remaining vulnerable to external impacts, making the understanding of head contact essential for human safety. Despite its importance, dense head-object contact estimation remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the absence of head-object contact data. Recently, it has been shown that synthetic data can serve as powerful training data in limited data scenario, implying the potential of synthetic data in head-object contact estimation. There are two core challenges for dense head-object contact estimation. First, head-object interactions are highly diverse, resulting in substantial variations in contact regions and patterns across different objects and interaction types. Second, head contact regions are often heavily occluded by hair, making direct visual observation of the actual contact regions difficult. To address these issues, we introduce HEad COntact estimation (HECO) with synthetic data. To handle diverse head-object interactions, we leverage semantic context from text features that encode semantic relationships between head regions and interacting objects. To resolve hair occlusion issue of actual head contact regions, we introduce occlusion-aware contact learning that learns to infer head contact beyond visible information from images via amodal inpainting. As a result, we enable head-object contact estimation with HECO trained with our synthetic dataset, overcoming the issue of absence of contact data. The codes will be released.

title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
authors: Y. Lu; L. Wang; S. Okada
abstract: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

title: Voyag: Joint Multi-Intent Detection and Execution-Relation Classification for In-Vehicle Voice Assistants
authors: Sen Luo
abstract: An in-vehicle voice assistant must decide not only which intents an utterance contains but also how co-active intents may be executed: concurrently, in a fixed order, or not at all without arbitration. We present Voyag, a single-forward decision model that jointly predicts ten controlled vehicle-intent slots and a three-way execution relation (parallel, sequential, mutually exclusive) over each co-active intent pair. Voyag combines a multilingual ModernBERT-style encoder (mmBERT-base, 306.9M parameters), a typed per-slot choice head, and a lightweight GroupCalibration relation head (1.61M parameters) that consumes marker hidden states, pooled context, explicit resource-requirement profiles, and symmetrized outer-product conflict features. All objectives are optimized in one joint loss: soft cross-entropy over slot choices, focal cross-entropy over relations, and a mutex-consistency penalty. On a synthetic Chinese vehicle-life benchmark with semantic scene-level splits and a leakage audit (30,017 / 3,473 / 5,000 groups), validation-only selection yields 0.9893 slot accuracy and 0.0526 expected calibration error over 50,000 slot decisions. Conditioned on gold intents, the relation head reaches 0.8548 accuracy, 0.8473 macro-F1, and 0.6062 mutually-exclusive recall over 4,000 pairs; end to end with one encoder forward it reaches 0.8530 accuracy and 0.8464 macro-F1. Against a two-stage rule pipeline, the aggregate end-to-end gain is small and borderline, so we claim no aggregate advantage; the learned head's advantage lies in sequential and parallel recall where surface rules are blind. We report rule baselines with a tautology disclosure and a held-out thermal conflict failure.

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

title: WaDiS: Boundary-Preserving Diffusion Segmentation via Multi-Scale Wavelet Conditioning and Frequency-Aware Gating
authors: Qiang Gao; Yi Wang; Yong Zhang; Bin Fang; Yong Li; Lan Du; Cunjian Chen
abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong potential in medical image segmentation due to their generative capabilities and robustness. However, existing methods often struggle to preserve fine anatomical boundaries and to retain multi-scale structural information due to the loss of spatial and frequency details during feature encoding, particularly in complex clinical imaging conditions. This work presents WaDiS, a wavelet-powered conditional latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that addresses these limitations through multi-scale wavelet conditioning and frequency-aware information filtering for boundary preservation. The model adopts a multi-scale wavelet conditioning encoder to retain rich structural features, leveraging its lossless nature to better preserve semantic priors critical to the diffusion process. In addition, a Frequency-Aware Gating Block (FAGB) is introduced into the skip connections of the diffusion U-Net, enabling adaptive spectral filtering and residual fusion to better emphasize boundary structures while reducing irrelevant content. To improve generalization across clinical domains, we adopt a structure-preserving color augmentation strategy during training. Specifically, global color statistics are transferred between samples in the LAB color space, allowing the model to decouple appearance from structure and focus more on anatomical shape rather than color bias. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaDiS consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and conventional segmentation methods, with notable improvements in boundary accuracy, robustness to noise, and generalization under color variation. The code for this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: STMemoLLM: A Spatial-Temporal Memory-Augmented LLM for Robust Traffic Forecasting
authors: Jian Zhou; Binqing Wu; Zongjiang Shang; Wanghui Qiu; Dongliang Cui; Chenxi Jin; Yue Yu; Xinyi Fu; Ling Chen
abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.

title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
authors: Xu Yuan; Pangjing Wu; Wenqi Fan; Qing Li
abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
authors: Yanju Chen; Ying Li; Bosi Zhang; Hanzhi Liu; Hongbo Wen; Yufei Ding; Yuan Tian; Yu Feng
abstract: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines
authors: Ilya Zakharov; Alexey Markin; Konstantin Ostroukhov; Alexey Perminov; Roham Koohestani; Ekaterina Koshchenko; Agnia Sergeyuk
abstract: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

title: Leveraging Binary Hashing for Scalable Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
authors: Leonardo Roque; Kuangyun Zhu; Louis-Adrien Dufrène; Quentin Lampin; Grégoire Lefebvre; Mohamad Assaad
abstract: Transmitting semantically structured embedding vectors over digital channels is costly in bit rate, while conven- tional vector quantization approaches face limitations in scalabil- ity, encoding complexity, and index assignment. This paper inves- tigates binary hashing techniques from the information retrieval literature as semantic indexing strategies for general-purpose networks. We study random Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) along with Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-, Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)-, and ITQ (Iterative Quantization)- based variants in a semantic communication pipeline over a Binary Symmetric Channel. Embeddings are compressed into binary codes, reconstructed through Hamming retrieval from a shared table, and evaluated on downstream classification. Ex- periments on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) and the Banking77 dataset show that data-dependent hashing improves upon random LSH, while ITQ refinement increases robustness to channel noise. Among the evaluated methods, CCA- ITQ achieves the best classification accuracy across the tested channel conditions. These results indicate that binary hashing is an efficient and scalable alternative to quantization-based embedding compression for semantic communications.

title: Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning Coding for Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
authors: Leonardo Roque; Louis-Adrien Dufrène; Quentin Lampin; Grégoire Lefebvre; Mohamad Assaad
abstract: Transmitting quantized semantic embeddings over a bit-flip channel requires a binary mapping that minimizes expected reconstruction distortion. The classical Binary Switching Algorithm (BSA) ($\mathcal{O}(K^3 \log K)$ for $K$ centroids) yields locally optimal assignments but ignores hierarchical bit significance, making it incompatible with Unequal Error Protection (UEP). We propose Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning (RSGP), which recursively bisects the centroid affinity graph along the Fiedler eigenvector so that early bits separate semantically distant groups while later bits refine local structure. RSGP runs in $\mathcal{O}(K^3)$ with no iterative outer loop, and is the only method studied to show a systematic positive UEP gain: protecting early bits over later ones improves accuracy for RSGP, while being neutral or harmful for unstructured assignments. Experiments on the Banking77 dataset and the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) confirm that RSGP consistently matches or exceeds BSA accuracy across codebook sizes and error profiles.

title: Scaling Channel-Adaptive Self-Supervised Learning
authors: Alice V. De Lorenci; Seungeun Yi; Theo Moutakanni; Piotr Bojanowski; Camille Couprie; Juan C. Caicedo; Wolfgang M. Pernice
abstract: Recent advances in self-supervised pre-training of foundation models for natural images have made them a popular choice for various visual systems and applications. Self-supervised strategies are also promising in non-RGB scientific imaging domains such as in biology, medical and satellite imagery, but their broader application is hampered by heterogeneity in channel composition and semantics between relevant datasets: two datasets may contain different numbers of channels, and these may reveal distinct aspects of an object or scene. Recent works on channel adaptive strategies report substantial advantages for those that account for variable channel compositions without sacrificing the ability to jointly encode channels; yet, how these strategies behave at scale remains unclear. We here show that, surprisingly, trained across large-scale datasets, independent-encoding of channels outperforms joint-encoding methods by a substantial margin. We validate this result along an extensive set of experiments on various datasets from cell microscopy to geospatial imagery. Our DINO BoC approach sets a new state-of-the-art across challenging benchmarks, including generalization to out-of-distribution tasks and unseen channel combinations. We open-source code and model weights for a new general-purpose feature extractor for fluorescent microscopy.

title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
authors: Zihan Pan; Jinghan Wang; Hang Li; Feng Cheng; Tianchen Liu; Gaoliang Peng
abstract: Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar-inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird's-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54-2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at: https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.

title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
authors: Peng Zheng; Deng-Ping Fan; Binglu Wang; Nicu Sebe
abstract: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet-V2.
